core.text: Deponents make their past with **the perfect of a deponent verb (locutus est = he spoke)**: the deponent participle plus the present of *sum*. *Ariadna Thēseum secūta est* — Ariadne followed Theseus; *profectī sunt* — they set out. The shape is exactly a perfect passive; the meaning is plain active past, because deponents always mean active. Latin name: *perfectum verbī dēpōnentis*.
Think of it as one verb, *followed*, even though Latin spells it with two words.
Participle (agreeing with the subject) + sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt = 'did'. Never translate with 'was' or 'been'.

*Laudātus est* and *locūtus est* are built the same way, but **the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudatus est)** means 'he was praised' while the deponent means 'he spoke'. The verb decides, not the form: look it up and see whether its infinitive ends in -ī.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 22) admit this form 'looks even more passive' to an English speaker because of the helping verb, and insist the translation is always active: *puer lāpsus est* — the boy slipped; *canis eum secūtus est* — the dog followed him.

Semi-deponents are active in the present but deponent in the perfect: *audeō, ausus sum* (dare), *gaudeō, gāvīsus sum* (rejoice), *soleō, solitus sum* (be used to). The pluperfect swaps in *erat*: *profectī erant* — they had set out.

teach.title: Two words, one plain past
teach.say: A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) makes its past out of two words, and the pair together is **the perfect of a deponent verb (locūtus est = he spoke)**. In *Mēdus ex vīllā statim profectus est* the two words *profectus est* say one thing: set out. Never put 'was' or 'been' into it — a deponent is active whatever it looks like.

teach.title: Where the two words come from
teach.say: The first word is the verb's perfect participle — *locūtus*, *secūtus*, *profectus* — and the second is the plain present of *sum*: *sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt*. In the table this is the column headed *deponent*, because the deponent has borrowed the passive's shape; only the shape. Read *secūta est* as if it were one word: followed.

show.say: secūtus est — the participle with est, in the column headed deponent

teach.title: The first word agrees with the subject
teach.say: The participle is an adjective, so it takes its ending from whoever did the action: *-us* for one man, *-a* for one woman, *-ī* for several men, *-ae* for several women. *Lȳdia … profecta est*, but *Nautae … ēgressī sunt*. The second word moves with it: *est* for one, *sunt* for more than one.

teach.title: Telling it from the perfect passive
teach.say: *Vocātus est* and *locūtus est* are built alike, and only the verb decides which is which. *Vocō* has an ordinary active present, so *vocātus est* is **the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudātus est)** — he was called. *Loquor* has no active at all, so *locūtus est* can only mean he spoke. Look the verb up: a dictionary infinitive ending in *-ī* or *-rī* rather than *-re* (*loquī* not *loquere*, *laetārī* not *laetāre*, *verērī* not *verēre*) marks a deponent.

teach.title: Reading it in a real sentence
teach.say: The two words often stand apart, with the object or an ablative between them, and the sense is unchanged: *Mīlitēs hostēs magnō clāmōre secūtī sunt*. Put it into English as a plain past — followed, spoke, set out, feared, slipped — and never reach for 'was'.
